Note for Trisha's mother, Sunday evening. At the house today, Trisha, two years old, stayed pressed against my legs while the grown-ups cried in the front room. Trisha kept looking at each face, thumb in mouth, and would not go to the toys. I did not send Trisha away. I picked Trisha up, held on and said quietly, "Everyone is sad about Dada. I am here." "Vaibhav, Nana's body stopped working. Nana died. He will not wake up, and he cannot return."

"No, beta. Sleeping bodies wake up. Nana's body has stopped. It doesn't hurt him now."
"Will you die?"
Usha took a breath. "One day, when I am very old. Not soon. I am here now."
Vaibhav leaned on her shoulder. Later, in the yard, he asked the same question again, and Usha answered the same way.

I'm Naveen, and I said the wrong thing at my friend Divyansh's grandfather's funeral. We were standing outside the hall, and Divyansh looked so lost. I wanted to help, so I blurted, "At least he lived a long life."
Divyansh's face closed. "Yeah," was all Divyansh said, and turned away to a cousin.

qa.a: Divyansh probably felt unheard and hurt, since the loss was still fresh. The closed face and short "Yeah" show it did not comfort.

Thursday night. Everyone keeps asking how I am and I keep saying "I'm fine." Papa died six weeks ago. I go to work, I answer emails, I laugh at the right moments. Inside there is a grey nothing and sometimes a hot anger at nothing at all. I don't tell anyone because they have their own lives.
